item.title: NWS: Get ready for tropical storm or low-end typhoon this weekend
item.description: Forecasters say Guam and the Northern Marianas should prepare for a tropical storm or low-end typhoon over the weekend as Tropical Depression 29W continues to organize and strengthen. The Joint Typhoon Warning Center indicates the storm will pass between Guam and Rota overnight Saturday and into Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters say Guam and the Northern Marianas should prepare for a tropical storm or low-end typhoon over the weekend as Tropical Depression 29W continues to organize and strengthen.

The Joint Typhoon Warning Center indicates the storm will pass between Guam and Rota overnight Saturday and into Sunday.

Patrick Bowsher of the National Weather Service says the storm is still far enough out that there is some uncertainty about its track and intensity.

Bowsher said the system could pass anywhere from the south of Guam to the north of Saipan.

He said it is expected to develop into a tropical storm by Friday and possibly reach typhoon strength by the weekend.

Residents are advised to prepare for strong winds, heavy rains and power outages.

item.title: Barnett calls for Won Pat's resignation as GDOE superintendent

Chris Barnett has called for the resignation of the Guam schools superintendent, but Judith Won Pat says she is not stepping down and would appreciate support from the Legislature. item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Barnett has called for the resignation of the Guam schools superintendent, but Judith Won Pat says she is not stepping down and would appreciate support from the Legislature.

Barnett sent Won Pat a letter criticizing recent problems in the schools, including the plan to put Simon Sanchez High School students in a shared campus at Tiyan, the failed sanitation inspection at Tiyan, double sessions and the brief loss of Western Association of Schools and Colleges accreditation.

Barnett raised questions about problems with communication between the Department of Education and parents, and said faculty and staff do not feel supported.

He said none of the problems began with Won Pat, but what he described as “lack of communication, backwards priorities and bad decisions” have not led to progress in the schools.

He asked for her resignation, effective immediately.

In response, Won Pat said she is not resigning but remains committed to leading the Guam Department of Education and to working hard for students, families, and employees.

She added that she would appreciate Barnett’s help with the department, as support for the legislature is essential to addressing the department’s needs.

item.title: Rematriated latte stone symbolizes resilience, identity, renewal

item.content:encoded:
Members of the Marianas High School Polksai Guma Chamorro Club performed traditional chants Wednesday morning during a rematriation ceremony at the NMI Museum of History & Culture, where cultural leaders welcomed home an ancient Åtchu’ Latti’ returned to the Marianas after more than a century.

The Northern Marianas Humanities Council and the museum hosted the event, marking the return of the latte stone originally taken from Rota in the early 20th century and held for decades in the Bishop Museum’s Hornbostel Collection.

The ceremony also included the signing of a proclamation designating October 2026 as CNMI Humanities Month.

Humanities Council Executive Director Leo Pangelinan said the homecoming reflects the community’s resilience and commitment to cultural stewardship, especially after recent storms and economic strain.

He tied the event to this year’s Humanities Month theme, Rooted in Heritage, Seeded to Flourish, noting that “resilience is knowing what sustains us.”

Lt. Gov. Dennis Mendiola signed the proclamation and urged families to preserve language, stories, and traditions for younger generations. He said the humanities live not only in institutions but in everyday cultural practice.

NMI Museum acting Board Chair Mona Mercado described the rematriation as “a return of spirit, memory, and belonging,” recounting the latte stone’s journey from Rota to Hawaii and its rediscovery by Saipan residents Martin and Linda Naputi. She said the museum will temporarily house the stone until its original site on Rota is identified.

Museum officials said the latte’s return was made possible through collaboration with the CNMI Historic Preservation Office, Bishop Museum, Guam Museum, Chamorro Affairs Office and the Guam Cultural Repository.

item.content:encoded:
As polar ice melts in the Arctic , shipping lanes are opening up , making the region a new zone of superpower competition. Writer Rana Foroohar got an up-close look aboard the USS Healy, a Coast Guard icebreaker. She says that traversing the North Pole by ship — once a "largely conceptual" route — is now becoming a "real possibility" for two or three weeks a year.

"If you are taking one of these Arctic routes, you can save as much as 40% of the time it would take you to go from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and depending on the price of oil, that's a heck of a lot of money," she says. "China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest."

In her new book, Sea Change: America's New Great Game in the Arctic Circle, Foroohar makes the case that the "High North" may become as critical to world shipping as the Suez or Panama canals . But she also notes that beneath the Arctic waters are large deposits of oil, natural gas and rare earth minerals, as well as underwater cables , which carry a large part of the world's intercontinental information flow.

"Undersea cables have become a real touchstone in wars and conflicts around the world," she says. "So you are seeing a race to lay down new cable, and who can get there fastest, and then who can potentially commercialize and even militarize areas where those cables have been laid."

Foroohar describes the Arctic Circle as one of the few areas of the globe where countries and companies can still "hunt" for territory and "duke it out potentially with rivals." And she predicts more conflict in the coming decades as the region continues to warm.

"There is going to be more commerce done through this area. There is gonna be greater military interest in the area, and all of that matters because it really is in America's backyard," she says. "I just think that everything in the High North is going to be higher priority for America in the future."

On increased international interest in the Arctic

China and Russia together are clearly trying to make the top of the world an area over which they have the most interest. And that's very interesting because it starts to dovetail with something that's happening in U.S. policy, which is more of a sense of we need to protect what's close to home. And so if you look at things that way, then you have the U.S. and China coming into much closer geographic conflict. Whether or not it would ever be a hot conflict, I hope not, but certainly competition in that area.

On the debate over rights to resources in international waters

There's some debate over that. There is something called the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea , which governs maritime activities, including those in the Arctic. It has ... rules about where you can mine, how you can mine, who gets what. But the U.S. never signed on to that convention. Various presidents from Clinton to Bush [to] Obama did support it, but key Republican senators opposed it, basically on ideological grounds, the notion that no international body should have sovereign right over what the U.S. does. ... And so it makes it much more of a free-for-all as to who gets what in the Arctic. And then you throw in the fact that Russians and Chinese don't always play by the U.N. rules either.

On how Arctic power struggles are part of a larger global trend

It's kind of part and parcel of a bigger collapse of international rule and a pendulum shift from globalization to something that is much more about regionalization and spheres of power ... and influence, which is exactly what's happening in the Arctic, which to me is so interesting, not only just for itself, but because it's a mirror into what's happening in other parts of the world. Some of the same conflicts over territory and mineral rights and ports that you see in the Arctic now are also happening in Latin America or West Africa or parts of the South China Sea. So it's a bit of a bellwether for geostrategy more broadly. …

And then there's this — kind of largely theoretical up until now, but becoming more realistic — trans-polar route where right now it might be a couple of weeks that you could consider going right across the pole, but if global warming continues the way it seems to be going in the next decade or two, that could turn into a month, two months, three months. And so who's going to control that area? This is what's up for stake now.

On what it's like to be onboard an Arctic icebreaker

You begin to feel and hear the ice as it is being broken by the ship. And I remember being down on the mess hall, which is a couple floors down from the waterline, and I was sitting eating my lunch and you begin to hear this shhhhhh kind of sound, like something traveling through sound, and then it becomes squeaky, like fingers on chalkboard, and you can kind of feel vibration and it gets louder and louder and you're like, "Wow, there are only 12 inches of reinforced steel between me and death." That's very sobering.

I actually touched base with some of those scientists several months after we had come off of the Healy, and they were starting to go through that data and look at it. And there is some real scientific data showing that these areas are changing. They are warming. They are becoming different than they have been in the past. And that affects all kinds of things. It affects the kind of fish that could live there. It affects wind and wave patterns that you might get, which could in turn affect things like the Canadian boreal forest fires that I experience in my home in Brooklyn, New York. You would think that has nothing to do with the Arctic, but it actually has everything to do with what's happening in the High North.

Therese Madden and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

item.content:encoded:
I've never cared much about cooking. Blame my mother. A woman of her generation, my mother never questioned that, even when she was working as a secretary, it was her job to get dinner (or "supper," as we called it) on the table every night for me and my father. She served up a meat and two veg most weeknights; Horn & Hardart fish cakes on Friday; and a roast on Sunday. But, she also often declared that she hated to cook.

This endless production line of hot meals occasionally ground to a halt. Whenever I had a half day off from school, my mother would pick me up and say, with guilty excitement, "Let's go into the city. I'll get Dad cold cuts for supper."

"The city," New York, was a quick subway ride away, and we'd wander around a department store or sometimes go ice skating in Rockefeller Center. Once in a while, we'd stop into a coffee shop for an early clandestine supper of our own: grilled cheese sandwiches and egg creams. Those escapades left me with an abiding love for New York and a belief that food was mostly just fuel for the more interesting things to do in life.

It turns out that Roz Chast and her friend, fellow New Yorker cartoonist Jason Adam Katzenstein, agree with me! They've co-authored a new graphic book called The Two Saddest Kitchens in which they chronicle, via what they call a "comics conversation," the fear and shame sparked by their own apartment kitchens and their lack of interest in cooking anything in them. (Chast, for the record, also has a home in Connecticut, where she seems to have replicated the existential despair of her city kitchen.)

Lest this subject sound off-putting to you enthusiastic home cooks out there, know that the great food writer and chef Ruth Reichl has blurbed this book, saying: "I don't think I've ever laughed so hard." I second that blurb. Who among us wouldn't at least smile at digressions here that speculate on the backstory of Mr. Clean and his less obsessive twin, "Mr. Clean Enough," or dare to explore what Chast calls "the saddest part of [her] kitchen," also known as, "the cabinet above the refrigerator," filled with "straws from 2004," "forgotten marshmallows," and a "pointlessly large bowl"?

Chast's and Katzenstein's senses of humor meld seamlessly: Both are master observers of what might be called the "uncanny mundane," where everyday objects reveal their inner weirdness. Take a cartoon by Katzenstein of a refrigerator shelf upon which sit two tiny plastic take-out containers. The thought bubble above one container reads: "He's coming back for me tomorrow — he just has to... " The cartoon is entitled: "The Very Delusional Takeout Sauce."

Those familiar with Chast's award-winning graphic memoir, Can't We Talk About Something More Pleasant? , about coping with her aging parents, will be glad to know they make cameo appearances here. Chast's mother, we're told, "shov[ed] a soft-boiled egg into [little Roz]" every day, believing eggs were "brain food" and, thus, leaving Chast with lifelong "texture issues" about "goopy" or "viscous" food.

Chast and Katzenstein occasionally turn their gaze to the city outside their kitchens. Intriguingly, they share anxieties about being infantilized by New York, given that it's what Katzenstein calls "the greatest takeout city on Earth." If eating takeout allows Chast and Katzenstein the time to create more original, unpretentious, and hilarious books like this one, I say, "Order on!"

item.title: Inflation sizzled in September — and Social Security benefits will get a boost
item.description: Nights are getting colder, but inflation is heating up. A report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago. That's a larger annual increase than the previous month.
item.content:encoded:
Nights are getting colder, but inflation is heating up.

A report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago. That's a larger annual increase than the previous month.

A spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran drove the cost of living higher. Prices jumped 0.6% between August and September.

"It's not looking good," said economist Brian Bethune of Boston College. "The main problem, of course, that everybody knows is gasoline prices. But also heating oil."

Heating oil is a close cousin of diesel fuel. The cost of the fuel oil has jumped 74% in the last year, which is hard on families in New England who rely on heating oil to stay warm.

Stripping out volatile energy and food prices, what's known as "core inflation" was 2.6% in September. That's also a bigger annual increase than was tallied in August.

The artificial intelligence boom has raised the cost of memory chips, affecting all sorts of consumer electronics. Apple, for example, raised the price of older-model iPhones last month by $100 apiece.

Shortly after the inflation report was released, the Social Security Administration announced that benefits will increase by 3.6% next year . The annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices in July, August and September.

The jump in benefits amounts to an extra $75 a month for the average Social Security recipient.

Advocates for seniors welcomed the increase.

"It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and other everyday expenses," said AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan.

But critics complain that the cost-of-living adjustment doesn't reflect seniors' actual expenses, which often include higher costs for healthcare.

"It won't be enough for most seniors to even tread water financially," said Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.

Treading water would be an improvement for most workers, whose paychecks are not keeping pace with today's rising prices.

Average wages in September rose just 3%, so the typical worker's buying power has eroded over the last year.

"People are kind of saying, 'Something isn't right with that,'" Bethune said. "I'm working harder. I'm more productive. And this is not a square deal."

Inflation is not nearly as high as it was in 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But every time prices start to level off, the economy is rattled by a new supply shock, such as President Trump's double-digit tariffs or the war with Iran.

Beth Hammack, who heads the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank, worries the cumulative effect of these shocks could make inflation more entrenched. Hammack told a group of economists this week about a Cleveland-area retailer she'd heard from who is raising prices not just to cover today's costs but the higher costs that may come in the future.

"This could be a sign that an inflationary mindset is taking hold," Hammack said. "When people expect higher prices, they make decisions with this in mind. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that makes it harder for monetary policy to bring inflation back down."

Policymakers at the Federal Reserve will weigh the new inflation data when they meet in two weeks to discuss interest rates. Investors now see about a 50-50 chance the Fed will raise its benchmark rate in October in an effort to combat inflation.

item.content:encoded:
Mario had his moment. Now it's Zelda's turn.

After The Super Mario Movie and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie made billions , Zelda is heading to the big screen next April . So to keep the franchise front and center, Nintendo is lavishly remaking its 1998 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time . The game debuts Nov. 5th, two weeks before the meteoric arrival of Grand Theft Auto VI — the only major release to dare compete with it that month.

As other companies dodge the Grand Theft Auto juggernaut by avoiding the November release window, Nintendo's wholesome throwback is poised to stand out against the glitzy violence of Grand Theft Auto . While many will play both games, the early holiday season offers a contrast : a family-friendly fantasy or a modern-day crime epic.

They're both gorgeous to look at. GTA' s Netflix preview showed off the obsessive photorealism developer Rockstar Games is known for. The Ocarina of Time remake, alternatively, maintains the original game's cartoony aesthetic but layers it with intricate detail.

Your tunic isn't just flat green; it's a hand-stitched jumble of embroidered fabrics and leathers. And fairies aren't just simple balls of light; they're furry creatures with mosaic wings. Yet, as someone who grew up with the original game and lost count of how many times I beat it, I found that the remake's baroque environments could confuse as well as dazzle.

Nintendo gave me 90 minutes to play through a cross-section of the game at a New York City preview. I blazed through Kokiri Forest, drinking in its dappled light and rippling waters. Then I dashed through Hyrule Field. Though it's tiny by today's gaming standards, it still felt as vast as I remembered thanks to clever atmospheric lightning. Castle Town bustled more than ever, teeming with banners, flowers and colorful citizenry. Even as I raced to explore as much as possible from the main plot, I couldn't help but stop to admire the scenery and shops of the city.

I was then thrown ahead to the Forest Temple — my favorite dungeon in the entire series. I was making good time and expected to reach its final boss before my session elapsed. Alas, I somehow skipped a chest containing the key I needed to progress. A Nintendo representative pointed me in the right direction, acknowledging that the rich details could overwhelm the eye and make it hard to know exactly where to go next.

I dwell on the game's aesthetic transformation because its mechanical changes are comparatively restrained. After all, why fix what's not broken? The original Ocarina of Time pioneered 3D video games and established action mechanics that still reign over the industry. Modest updates hit the game when it was repackaged for the GameCube and 3DS. For the Switch 2, Nintendo is applying a user interface reminiscent of 2017's The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and a quest log in the pause menu called "Threads of Time." It's also adding movement features I almost forgot were missing: a jump and a sprint.

In the original Ocarina of Time , you'd automatically jump when you ran off a ledge or gap. While you can choose to keep the old control scheme, the game now allows you to hop on command. It's not too useful in combat, but I did manage to jump to the roof of a forest hut otherwise only accessible through a winding footpath. Don't expect Breath of the Wild openness. The game still seems to be a linear adventure, just one that now allows the occasional vertical shortcut. Also, you can hold a button to sprint, a boon to those who constantly rolled around because it was faster than jogging.

While I've protested Nintendo remakes before, I'll readily admit that Ocarina of Time is not just a safe bet but a smart one. With Zelda so close to its movie debut, the game's poised to ensnare old fans and entice new players. Its sky-high production values also fit a new priority for the company, which has lavished attention on animation as well as gameplay since 2023's Super Mario Bros. Wonder .

The Ocarina of Time remake is the prettiest Zelda game I've ever played. But I'll need more than a 90-minute preview to see if its beauty is more than skin deep.
